sections.title: Towers in a high mountain valley
sections.body: Upper Svaneti lies in the Georgian Caucasus, where settlements sit beneath steep ridges and snow-covered peaks. Families built distinctive stone towers beside houses in villages that could be difficult to reach for much of the year. The landscape combines domestic architecture with pastures, rivers and mountain passes. Its isolation helped preserve buildings, but it never meant that the communities lacked contacts or a history of exchange.

sections.title: Buildings made for everyday life
sections.body: The towers served defensive functions, while adjoining houses provided space for people, equipment and, traditionally, livestock. Their construction reflects family organisation and the practical challenges of mountain living. Churches and painted interiors also preserve evidence of religious and artistic traditions. These buildings should not be treated as anonymous scenery: local Svan communities have maintained relationships with them across generations.

sections.title: Land and climate
sections.body: The upper Enguri basin contains sharply contrasting heights and environments. Snowfall and difficult winter routes influence travel, agriculture and repairs. Small fields and pastures show how settlement patterns developed around available land, rather than following a regular urban grid. Conservation therefore needs to consider paths, drainage, climate and working land alongside the famous towers themselves.

sections.title: A living heritage landscape
sections.body: The importance of Svaneti comes from the connection between village buildings and their surrounding mountains. Replacing traditional materials carelessly or allowing historic structures to deteriorate could weaken that relationship. The UNESCO property covers a particular part of Upper Svaneti, not every settlement in Georgia. It offers one way to understand how architecture adapts to social needs and remote landscapes.

sections.title: A Pyrenean valley shaped by use
sections.body: The Madriu-Perafita-Claror Valley in Andorra includes steep wooded slopes, open high pastures and remnants of glacial landforms. Its protected area covers a sizeable part of this small principality. Unlike a site defined by one castle or town square, the valley preserves clues about how people worked with mountain resources over centuries. Stone paths, huts and terraced fields make that history visible.

sections.title: Pastoral life and communal land
sections.body: Seasonal grazing involved moving animals between valley levels as weather and pasture conditions changed. Communities organised access to land and resources through customary arrangements that survived for many generations. Small shelters, walls and places where hay or tools were stored speak to this everyday work. The landscape tells a story of practical decisions, not of a mountain environment untouched by people.

sections.title: Routes, iron and energy
sections.body: The valley also contains evidence of past metalworking, including traces linked to the Catalan forge. Moving fuel, ore and finished materials in mountainous terrain required skills and transport routes. These industrial traces sit alongside agricultural ones, showing that mountain economies were more varied than herding alone. The absence of roads through much of the protected area makes the older path network especially revealing.

sections.title: Preserving a relationship with land
sections.body: Conservation depends on maintaining historic features while recognising the changing needs of residents and visitors. The glacial landscape, built structures and forms of communal management are related parts of the heritage. Studying their connection helps explain how highland communities made a living in difficult conditions, and why the disappearance of traditional practices can matter as much as damage to stone.

sections.title: A city around the Vltava
sections.body: Prague developed along both banks of the Vltava River, with hilltop fortifications, bridges and neighbourhoods growing over centuries. Its historic centre contains Old Town, Lesser Town and New Town, alongside the castle complex. These areas are not all the same age. Their streets and buildings preserve evidence of political decisions, commercial life and changing ideas about how an important European city should function.

sections.title: A medieval plan with later layers
sections.body: Charles IV helped shape the city's fourteenth-century development, including the New Town and major building projects. Gothic churches and the bridge remain visible, but Romanesque, Baroque and later structures complicate the skyline. Preservation has retained substantial sections of the older street pattern. Looking from one square to another reveals several eras rather than a single medieval reconstruction.

sections.title: Exchange and everyday life
sections.body: Prague was a centre of trade, learning and craft production, with religious and cultural communities contributing to its development. Palaces express elite patronage, whereas houses and lanes reveal the activities of less prominent residents. The Jewish Quarter is another important part of the city's history. A responsible account should not let picturesque architecture obscure changes in social life, exclusion or periods of conflict.

sections.title: A working capital
sections.body: Today the historic centre must accommodate housing, transport, visitors and heritage protection. The river also remains part of the city's geography and flood management. The strongest way to read Prague is through its urban layout and connections: bridges join districts, streets link markets and institutions, and building styles show centuries of adaptation.

sections.title: A trading town above the Baltic
sections.body: Tallinn's old town sits near the Baltic Sea, with an upper settlement on a limestone hill and a lower town around streets and market spaces. Its towers and walls show how merchants and authorities protected an important port. The preserved medieval street pattern is more than a backdrop for tourism; it reflects how a northern European trading city organised commerce and everyday life.

sections.title: The Hanseatic connection
sections.body: Tallinn, historically known as Reval, took part in the Hanseatic trading network. Merchants exchanged goods across the Baltic and inland routes, bringing wealth and architectural influences into the town. Merchant houses, warehouses and public buildings survive from different stages of that history. Sea access was central to economic growth, but the city's population also depended on hinterland supplies and labour.

sections.title: Two levels of the city
sections.body: Toompea's elevated position created a natural defensive location, while streets below served other trading and residential functions. Churches and town buildings developed through many centuries, including later renovations after fire or war. The resulting skyline should not be understood as perfectly unchanged since the Middle Ages. Restoration and continued use have both influenced the surviving buildings.

sections.title: Keeping a lived-in centre
sections.body: Modern Tallinn is much larger than its old town, and the historic district remains subject to pressures from tourism and changing land use. Conservation must consider local residents alongside masonry and roofs. A walk between the hill and lower streets shows how geography, politics and trade shaped the city. It offers a clear example of urban heritage made through ordinary commerce as well as monumental construction.

records.hook: Hungary — Budapest and the Danube Banks

sections.title: Two banks of one capital
sections.body: Budapest extends along the Danube, with hilly Buda on the western bank and flatter Pest to the east. The river gives the city its central urban axis and has influenced defence, trade and transport. The World Heritage property includes the riverbanks, the Buda Castle Quarter and Andrássy Avenue. Its distinct parts reflect several periods of urban development rather than one unified architectural plan.

sections.title: Cities linked by bridges
sections.body: Historic Buda and Pest had different landscapes and roles before becoming parts of the modern capital. Bridges helped change how people moved between them, while nineteenth-century urban growth transformed public spaces. The castle quarter retains earlier layers, whereas grand boulevards and civic buildings show later ambitions. Looking across the river makes the contrast between the two banks especially visible.

sections.title: Politics, culture and rebuilding
sections.body: Budapest's monuments have been altered by political change, damage and reconstruction. Palaces and institutions present only part of the history; housing, industry and transport also shaped everyday life. The riverfront was never purely ceremonial. Residents used it for crossings, movement of goods and city services. A full account must recognise both architectural achievement and the disruptions experienced by the city.

sections.title: A changing riverside
sections.body: The Danube remains important for water management, movement and urban identity. Conservation decisions affect buildings, sightlines and the character of public spaces. Budapest shows how a major river can organise city growth over long periods, while the surrounding built environment continues to change. Understanding the site begins with the geography of Buda and Pest rather than with one famous facade.

sections.title: Streets at a meeting of rivers
sections.body: Vilnius developed in a valley near the Neris and Vilnia rivers. Its winding roads and squares preserve a medieval street pattern, while later churches, townhouses and university buildings reflect changing political and cultural connections. The historic centre is not arranged around one monumental axis. Its varied districts suggest gradual adaptation to terrain, communities and trade routes.

sections.title: Different religious traditions
sections.body: Over the centuries the city became home to several religious and linguistic communities, with Catholic, Orthodox and Jewish histories all leaving marks on its institutions and built fabric. Surviving buildings offer evidence, but many important sites were damaged or destroyed during war and occupation. Responsible interpretation includes absent places and lives, not only the attractive structures still standing.

sections.title: Urban culture and learning
sections.body: The university and surrounding buildings helped shape Vilnius as a centre of education and intellectual exchange. Gothic, Renaissance, Baroque and later architecture often sit close together, showing successive periods of rebuilding. Political changes involving the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and later states affected the city, although no one historical government explains its entire appearance. Streets are valuable evidence of continuity amid those shifts.

sections.title: Conservation beyond facades
sections.body: The current city must balance residents, transport, development and tourism with heritage protection. The UNESCO property is recognised partly for the remarkable survival of its spatial plan. Look at routes between churches and markets, the differences in street widths and views across rooflines. These details explain how a historic capital develops without requiring every building to belong to the same era.

sections.title: A Baltic city of layers
sections.body: Riga developed beside the Daugava River, connecting inland territories with Baltic shipping routes. Its medieval centre was part of the Hanseatic trading world, but much of the city now visible dates from later periods of growth. Streets, churches and warehouses sit near nineteenth- and early twentieth-century districts. Together they show how trade and expansion reshaped a port city over hundreds of years.

sections.title: The age of Art Nouveau
sections.body: Riga is well known for its extensive Jugendstil or Art Nouveau architecture. Decorative building fronts reflect an era of rapid urban growth, professional design and investment. These structures often contain ordinary flats and businesses rather than palaces. Their value lies partly in showing how an architectural style entered the fabric of everyday city life. Not every ornate facade belongs to precisely the same artistic school or date.

sections.title: Earlier networks and influences
sections.body: The old town preserves connections to German-speaking merchants and other communities, while Latvian social and cultural life also developed through the city's changing political circumstances. Fire, war and redevelopment affected what survived. Riga's history should not be reduced to either its medieval trading role or its Art Nouveau streets. Those are different chapters connected by the same river and urban economy.

sections.title: A centre still in use
sections.body: Modern development raises questions about conserving older districts while meeting residents' needs. The most revealing comparison is between the irregular street network of the medieval core and planned streets nearby. Their differences show how planning, commerce and cultural identity changed. Riga is an example of urban heritage surviving through adaptation rather than staying fixed at one chosen date.

sections.title: A city on steep rock
sections.body: Luxembourg City's historic core developed where the Alzette and Pétrusse valleys cut into a plateau. The steep landform gave defenders an advantage and encouraged the growth of extensive walls, tunnels and fortified positions. Its geography is immediately apparent from viewpoints over the lower valleys. Much of the military landscape no longer stands, yet the surviving structures still reveal the scale of earlier engineering.

sections.title: Competing powers and changing defences
sections.body: The fortress was repeatedly strengthened as different European states controlled the area. Builders adapted bastions and underground works to changing military technology. These additions took place over several centuries, so the surviving fabric should not be attributed to a single ruler or architect. Fortification shaped roads, access and everyday movement, influencing the whole settlement rather than forming a ring of isolated monuments.

sections.title: The dismantling of a stronghold
sections.body: During the nineteenth century, significant sections of the fortress were dismantled, altering the city's appearance and potential for development. Some defensive works were retained, while former military areas took on new uses. The remaining landscape therefore illustrates both construction and deliberate removal. Looking at a modern street can reveal where an older wall or gate once directed movement.

sections.title: A capital with layered roles
sections.body: Luxembourg today is known for political and financial institutions, but its fortified heritage belongs to a different set of European relationships. Residents and planners must manage a historic centre built into difficult terrain. Studying the old quarters alongside the valleys makes clear that geology, strategic importance and urban development have long interacted in shaping the city.

sections.title: A fortified capital on a peninsula
sections.body: Valletta sits between two natural harbours on Malta's north-eastern coast. Following the sixteenth-century siege, the Knights of St John developed a planned city with strong defences, public buildings and a regular street network. Its narrow peninsula gave engineers both an opportunity and a challenge. The steep streets and bastions reveal how urban design responded to maritime security and topography.

sections.title: A city of institutions
sections.body: Churches, hospitals, palaces and civic spaces reflect the religious and military order that helped build Valletta. The city's heritage includes an unusual concentration of monuments, but it should not be understood as a uniform collection of grand buildings. Workshops, houses and service spaces were required to maintain everyday life. Successive generations altered the built environment after the original planning period.

sections.title: Harbours and connections
sections.body: The Grand Harbour and Marsamxett Harbour influenced trade, defence and movement around the islands. Naval power and international contacts shaped Valletta's history, while Malta's wider culture includes many periods before and after the Knights. The town plan is one chapter in that longer story. From the waterfront, its walls make physical sense as features controlling approach and access.

sections.title: Managing a dense historic centre
sections.body: Valletta remains Malta's capital and a place where people live and work. Conservation involves housing, transport, changing commercial activity and care for weathered limestone. The site's value rests partly in the coherence of its urban layout. Reading the streets together with the surrounding sea explains how planning and geography produced a fortified city that continues to serve civilian purposes.

records.focus: Natural and Culturo-Historical Region of Kotor
records.hook: Montenegro — Natural and Culturo-Historical Region of Kotor

sections.title: A historic town in a steep inlet
sections.body: Kotor lies at the end of a dramatic Adriatic inlet, enclosed by mountains and narrow coastal land. Its walls and urban fabric were shaped by the need to protect a trading settlement where ships could approach close to the mountains. The wider World Heritage region includes landscape and related communities, not just the streets of the old town.

sections.title: Seafaring and buildings
sections.body: Maritime trade connected Kotor with wider Adriatic networks, and Venetian influence is evident in periods of its architecture and public space. Churches and domestic buildings reflect different traditions and episodes of prosperity. The city developed under several political authorities; describing it as belonging to one permanent cultural identity would flatten a complicated history. Its surviving monuments are evidence of exchange as well as defence.

sections.title: Earthquakes and repair
sections.body: The region lies in a seismically active part of the Mediterranean. Damage from earthquakes, including the major 1979 event, required substantial conservation work. This is important because a restored historic district can still be authentic when documented repairs preserve significant features. Modern development also affects views across the inlet and the relationship between built heritage and the coastline.

sections.title: The whole setting matters
sections.body: An elevated view makes the close connection between mountain slopes, defensive walls and water especially clear. Kotor's heritage is not complete without the surrounding bay and settlements. Managing cruise visitors, transport and new construction creates ongoing choices about conserving the character of this narrow coastal landscape while allowing people to continue living and working there.

sections.title: A monastery in central Serbia
sections.body: Studenica was established in the late twelfth century and became an important centre of Serbian Orthodox religious life. Its main churches are built with striking stonework, within a walled monastic complex near wooded hills and river valleys. The site connects architecture with political and religious history, but it is also a place with continuing spiritual significance rather than a deserted medieval monument.

sections.title: Architecture and painting
sections.body: The Church of the Virgin and the King's Church preserve important paintings and architectural details. Influences from Byzantine and Romanesque traditions appear together, revealing cultural links that crossed modern national boundaries. The art can offer clues about patronage and religious belief, although dates and meanings still require careful scholarship. The structures were shaped by skilled builders and artists, not only by the rulers whose names appear in accounts.

sections.title: History beyond the walls
sections.body: Monastic communities depended on food, materials, land and relationships with nearby settlements. Remains associated with quarrying and older routes help place the complex within a working environment. The site's role in Serbian history is substantial, yet a whole country cannot be understood from its religious architecture alone. Different communities and regions experienced medieval political change in varied ways.

sections.title: Care for a living institution
sections.body: Preserving wall paintings, stone and timber requires control of moisture, weathering and visitor pressure. Religious practice must also be respected when access and interpretation are planned. Studenica offers a focused example of how religious institutions preserve art and historical memory while continuing to adapt to practical conservation needs.

sections.title: A river enters the karst
sections.body: In south-western Slovenia, the Reka River disappears underground through a remarkable limestone cave system. Its passages include a large subterranean canyon, enormous chambers and waterfalls. Water has dissolved and eroded the rock over long periods, creating landforms that helped establish the international study of karst. The caves show that a river landscape can continue far below the visible surface.

sections.title: Geology in motion
sections.body: Rainfall and upstream river conditions affect flows underground. Caverns, sinkholes and collapsed dolines record different stages of erosion and structural change. These features are not merely picturesque formations; they provide evidence of how limestone interacts with moving water. Observing the underground channel helps explain why water quality and land use far beyond the cave entrances affect conditions within the protected area.

sections.title: Habitat and fragility
sections.body: Caves provide specialised environments with low light, limited food and stable microclimates in certain passages. Bats and smaller organisms can depend on these conditions. Guided access reduces some risks, but foot traffic, artificial lighting and pollution must still be managed. Conservation cannot end at the cave entrance because groundwater and the river system connect the site to surrounding communities and industries.

sections.title: A landscape with two levels
sections.body: The surface plateau and deep cave passages tell one connected geological story. Studying them together reveals how an apparently ordinary landscape can contain vast hidden spaces. Škocjan is significant for scientific understanding as well as visitor experience, and responsible interpretation avoids suggesting that all passages are open or safe to enter independently.
